name: The Kingdom of Dahomey
title: Social Hierarchy of the Kingdom of Dahomey: From King to Enslaved
period: 1727–1894 (from the conquest of Whydah to the French conquest)

tiers.name: The king
tiers.you: You are the ahosu, heir of the kings of Allada; each year at the Annual Customs you receive the tribute of every lineage, honour your ancestors and close the Great Council’s debates by declaring its consensus.
tiers.kid: The king of Dahomey lived at Abomey, where each king built his own palace with pictures on its walls.
tiers.rise: Kingship passed through the male line, usually but not always to the eldest son, and the Great Council’s discussions largely decided the choice: Tegbesu, not the eldest, won a succession struggle with a brother in 1740, and Ghezo came to the throne in 1818 in place of his brother Adandozan.
tiers.why: The king, the ahosu, was the sovereign of Dahomey, and all the kings claimed descent from the royal family of Allada.

tiers.name: Great officers of the court
tiers.term: migan, mehu, yovogan, tokpo, agan, kpojito, chacha
tiers.you: You are the migan, the king’s chief counsellor and a leading judge, and his head executioner; in war you command the right of the army, and a woman holds your office’s counterpart.
tiers.kid: The king’s chief ministers ran the courts, the palaces, farming and the army, and each had a woman partner.
tiers.rise: The kpojito owed her place to her son: Hwanjile, a wife of Agaja, became the first significant kpojito when her son Tegbesu was king. The chacha’s title went to Francisco Félix de Sousa, a former enslaved man turned slave trader, after Ghezo came to the throne.
tiers.why: The king’s court was led by great officers.

tiers.name: Chiefs and royal officials
tiers.you: The king appointed you chief of your village; you settle its disputes, the tax officials count its harvest, and each year you go to Abomey for the Customs and the Great Council.
tiers.kid: The king chose chiefs to run each village and officials to count the harvest and collect taxes.
tiers.rise: Chiefs and officials held their posts by the king’s appointment, and at the Annual Customs they received gifts for their services.
tiers.why: Dahomey’s main political divisions were its villages, whose chiefs and officials the king appointed to act as his representatives and settle disputes.

tiers.name: Vodun priests and priestesses
tiers.you: You serve at the shrine of one of the gods of thunder, and your own family’s ceremonies for its ancestors must wait until the king’s Annual Customs are over.
tiers.kid: Priests and priestesses looked after the shrines of Dahomey’s many gods.
tiers.rise: The sources say little about how priests were made, except that the chief priest had to be of Dakodonu’s line.
tiers.why: Dahomey’s religion joined older animist traditions to Vodun.

tiers.name: Soldiers
tiers.you: You joined the army at eight as a shield carrier; now you carry a flintlock in the king’s standing army, and every captive you bring back earns you cowries.
tiers.kid: Dahomey’s soldiers trained from boyhood and were rewarded with cowrie shells.
tiers.rise: Boys entered at seven or eight as shield carriers and rose by service and by the captives they took; Ghezo also recruited soldiers from foreign captives.
tiers.why: From at least the time of Agaja Dahomey kept a professional standing army, encamped wherever the king was: about 10,000 strong by one account, 15,000 by another, divided into right, left, centre and reserve and into…

tiers.name: Women soldiers
tiers.you: You were chosen from the daughters the king required of every family; legally his wife, you may not bear children or live a married life, but you may rise to command and speak in the Great Council.
tiers.kid: Dahomey had an army of women soldiers who trained very hard and were respected in the kingdom.
tiers.rise: Women entered by capture, by the king’s levy of daughters, as a punishment or of their own will, and could rise to command; the corps was largely wiped out at Adegon in 1892 and disbanded in 1894.
tiers.why: The women soldiers were called Agojie or Mino (“our mothers”) and called themselves ahosi, the king’s wives; Europeans named them after the Amazons of Greek myth.

tiers.name: Traders and craftsmen
tiers.you: You trade at Whydah under the king’s licence and keep your cowries, and your neighbours’, in the strong hut in your compound.
tiers.kid: Craftspeople in Dahomey made carvings, brass figures and colourful cloth pictures, and traders sold goods in busy markets.
tiers.rise: Trade made fortunes, but at the king’s pleasure, since a private trader needed his licence to trade at Whydah; the palm oil plantations of the 19th century opened a new road to wealth.
tiers.why: Craftwork was dominated by a formal guild system, and blacksmiths, weavers and wood cutters paid taxes on their work.

tiers.name: Free farmers
tiers.you: You farm with your family and bring your lineage’s tribute to the Annual Customs at Abomey, where the king displays it and gives much of it back.
tiers.kid: Most people in Dahomey were farmers who brought gifts to the king at a great yearly festival.
tiers.rise: A family’s sons could enter the army as boys and its daughters could be levied for the women’s corps; criminals could be pressed into the corps or killed at the Annual Customs.
tiers.why: Most people were free farmers and their families: farming was done by most families, for local use until palm oil was exported.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You were captured in a raid on your town; you may be marched round the Tree of Forgetfulness and sold at Whydah, or kept to work the king’s palm oil plantations.
tiers.kid: Dahomey captured people in wars and sold many of them as slaves to European traders.
tiers.rise: Watson and Schellinger argue that slaves were once treated as members of their master’s family and could become free within a generation or two, but that the palm oil plantations made slavery harsher; Ghezo had the murders of slaves tried at the court in Abomey.
tiers.why: Dahomey’s growth went with the Atlantic slave trade.
